title: What he copied from Coltrane
summary: He studied Trane's sound, vibrato and solos, and his later albums.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: I’m trying to form a question here about what did you try to copy?

Oh boy, Trane, I mean the sound was one of the things that I’ve always been drawn to. His use of vibrato in the later period, you know where he was almost into a classical vibrato. You know when I studied at Berklee with Joe Viola, he stressed classical etudes

but not playing in that style. And so what I was always listening to the way Trane would use his vibrato, where he would play — usually a jaw vibrato but sometimes a jaw and a diaphragm combination vibrato. I heard Sonny Rollins doing the same thing where they combine the flute — ha-ha-ha-ha-ha — with the ya-ya-ya-ya jaw, so you get two things working at once. You get the depth of the stomach vibrato — ha-ha-ha-ha — that’s going here and there. It’s kind of tricky. I just picked it up. But I mean I just copied a lot of his solos, not in total but like what was that phrase, and I would listen to what’s that idea. I would pick little devices out to see if there were things that I liked.
Did he ever go out too far, you know in his last year or so, for you to keep up with?

There were times when, you know like one of my, let’s see “Expression,” that album, there’s one there I really like from that period back and then forwards, the other ones like “Om” and some of those other ones — “Live in Seattle” there’s some things that I like. But there was a point where I decided I’m going to listen to all of that stuff and see what he’s trying to get across in there. You know I always studied it, being an educator also. I mean I always wanted to kind of understand what’s going on with him. Some of it I didn’t like all the time, but I always enjoyed the way he played. Not always the combination of instruments that he had, I could see he was searching for a certain thing. Everything didn’t appeal to me. But most of it did.
